title: The FCA's Mills Review Expects AI to Move Retail Finance From Human-Led to Delegated Services and Makes Seven Priority Recommendations, Keeping the Consumer Duty at the Core
summary: The Financial Conduct Authority published the Mills Review on July 6, 2026, an independent review led by Sheldon Mills of how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030 and beyond; it identifies four systemic shifts, judges the current outcomes-based regime broadly fit for purpose and makes seven priority recommendations.
description:
On July 6, 2026, the UK Financial Conduct Authority published The Mills Review, a report on how artificial intelligence could change retail financial services over the coming years. The report is based on an independent review led by Sheldon Mills, the FCA's Executive Director for Consumers and Competition, and looks ahead to 2030 and beyond. This article is based on a summary published by the law firm A&O Shearman, not on the FCA's full text, so it covers the headline conclusions and recommendations and says plainly where detail is missing. The summary did not include any direct quotation from Mr Mills, details of what the FCA will do next, or a timetable.

The central conclusion

The review's main finding, in the words quoted in the summary, is that AI is likely to drive a transition from human-led financial activity to increasingly AI-enabled and delegated services. Two parts of that sentence matter. First, firms are expected to embed AI across many of their functions, not just in customer-facing chat tools. Second, consumers are expected to use AI tools and agents to manage their finances, which means that software could compare products, switch accounts or make payments on a person's behalf. The word delegated is important: if a customer hands a decision to an AI agent, questions arise about who is responsible when the outcome is poor.

Four systemic shifts

The review groups its analysis into four shifts. The summary lists them as headings, and the one-line glosses below are general explanations of the terms rather than the review's own findings.

AI becoming central to how firms operate. Instead of being an add-on, AI would be part of underwriting, credit assessment, fraud detection, servicing and decision-making.

AI-led consumer journeys. More of the path from a customer's question to a purchase would run through AI-driven interfaces, possibly operated by third parties instead of the financial firm.

Changes to competition and market power. The summary lists this as a shift without giving detail. The specifics are in the full report.

Greater financial crime and cyber risk. AI can be used by criminals as well as by firms, and more automated, connected systems create more points of attack.

The existing framework

One of the more notable conclusions is that the review does not call for the existing rulebook to be thrown out. It considers the current outcomes-based regime broadly fit for purpose. That regime includes the Consumer Duty, which requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers; the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, which makes named senior individuals accountable for areas of a firm's business; and operational resilience requirements, which set expectations for firms to withstand disruption. The review says these tools need to evolve to keep pace with AI, rather than being replaced.

The seven priority recommendations

According to the summary, which paraphrases them, the recommendations are:

First, secure and adapt the regulatory perimeter. The perimeter is the boundary that decides which activities need FCA authorisation. If AI agents and platforms start to perform activities that are close to regulated advice or distribution, the boundary may need to be reviewed.

Second, strengthen system-wide coordination and oversight. AI affects competition, data, cyber security and consumer protection, which sit with different authorities, so the review calls for better coordination.

Third, monitor the move toward autonomous models and adapt rules accordingly. The summary does not say how autonomy is currently distributed.

Fourth, scale up the FCA's AI Lab, the regulator's programme for engaging with AI developers and firms.

Fifth, enable the foundations for agentic finance, meaning the standards and infrastructure needed for AI agents to act safely for consumers.

Sixth, build and adopt an AI-enabled, agentic supervisory model, so that the regulator itself uses AI in supervising firms.

Seventh, develop a trusted, public-interest AI-enabled financial capability service, which would help consumers make better decisions with AI support.

The explanations added to the recommendations above are general descriptions of the terms, not statements of what the review says in detail; the summary lists the titles only.

What is missing and what to watch

The summary does not say how the FCA will respond to the recommendations, whether legislation or rule changes would be needed, or who will take each action. It also does not describe what the review says about accountability when an AI agent makes a mistake, which is probably the question that matters most to consumers. The report also looks to 2030, so many of its predictions are expectations rather than present facts, and the summary notes no caveats about uncertainty.

For firms, the practical message is that the regulator is likely to keep applying the Consumer Duty and senior manager accountability to AI-driven services, and to expect firms to understand and control the systems they use. For consumers, the review does not change rights today. Anyone who uses an AI tool for financial decisions should check who is providing the service and whether it is a regulated firm. Readers who need the exact recommendations should consult the FCA's published report. This article is general information and not legal advice.
source_name: A&O Shearman FinReg (summary of the FCA's Mills Review, published July 6, 2026)

key_points: The FCA published the Mills Review on July 6, 2026; it is based on an independent review led by Sheldon Mills, the FCA's Executive Director for Consumers and Competition, of how AI could affect retail financial services by 2030 and beyond.

Its core conclusion is that AI is likely to drive a transition from human-led financial activity to increasingly AI-enabled and delegated services, with consumers using AI tools and agents to manage their finances.
It identifies four systemic shifts: AI becoming central to how firms operate, AI-led consumer journeys, changes to competition and market power, and greater financial crime and cyber risk.

The review considers the current outcomes-based regime, including the Consumer Duty, the Senior Managers and Certification Regime and operational resilience rules, broadly fit for purpose but in need of evolving as AI advances.

Its seven priority recommendations cover the regulatory perimeter, system-wide coordination, monitoring autonomous models, scaling the FCA's AI Lab, foundations for agentic finance, an AI-enabled supervisory model and a public-interest financial capability service.
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and investment firms in the UK are already using AI, and consumers are starting to ask AI tools to compare products and manage money. The review shows the direction the UK regulator is thinking in: keep the existing outcomes-based rules, but adapt perimeter, coordination and supervision for a world in which software acts on a customer's behalf.

title: French Insurers' €2.85 Trillion Portfolio Absorbed €33.7 Billion of Valuation Losses in Q1 2026 as Long-Term Rates Rose, Offsetting Almost All New Investment
summary: Banque de France data show French insurers and pension funds held €2,854.5 billion of financial investments at end-Q1 2026; net inflows of €34.9 billion were offset by €33.7 billion of valuation losses from rising long-term rates, and a look-through view shows 26% of holdings are equities.
description:
French insurers and pension funds ended the first quarter of 2026 with financial investments of €2,854.5 billion, but a rise in long-term interest rates meant that almost all of their new investment was cancelled out on paper by falling asset values. The figures come from the Banque de France, which published its quarterly statistics on the financial investments of insurance corporations and pension funds on July 7, 2026 (updated July 17). The next publication was scheduled for October 6, 2026.

The headline arithmetic is simple. Insurers made net investments of €32.7 billion in the quarter, and pension funds added €2.2 billion, a combined €34.9 billion of new money. Against that, valuation effects were -€33.7 billion. The Banque de France attributes the valuation losses to rising long-term rates, which lowered bond prices, and to falling share prices. In other words, the portfolio barely grew in value over the quarter even though a great deal of fresh money was invested.

The breakdown by segment shows where the effect fell. Life and composite insurers, which hold most of the money because they manage life insurance savings and retirement products, held €2,354.0 billion at the end of the quarter. They invested €29.5 billion net but suffered valuation effects of -€28.6 billion. Non-life insurers, which write car, home and commercial cover, held €299.1 billion, with net flows of €3.2 billion and valuations of -€2.5 billion. Pension funds held €201.3 billion, with net flows of €2.2 billion and valuations of -€2.6 billion. The loss is therefore concentrated in the life segment, simply because that is where the assets are.

What did insurers buy? Before applying the look-through approach, the Banque de France reports direct purchases of long-term debt securities of €20.9 billion. Insurers also put €14.4 billion into investment fund shares, including €8.3 billion into non-money-market funds. Net flows into listed shares were -€2 billion, meaning insurers were net sellers. The pattern suggests a preference for fixed income at a time when bond yields were rising, which allows new money to lock in higher returns, together with continued use of funds as a way to gain diversified exposure.

The look-through view gives a fuller picture of what the portfolio holds. French funds are a major route for insurers' investments, so the Banque de France applies a look-through approach, treating the securities inside French funds as if the insurer held them directly. This changes the picture a good deal. The share of equities rises from 10% to 26% of the total, and the share of debt securities from 50% to 64%. About 1% remains in fund units that cannot be looked through, mainly foreign funds. By issuer, about 40% of the portfolio consists of securities issued by the financial sector excluding mutual funds, split between 25% other financial institutions and 15% monetary financial institutions such as banks. Geographically, about 41% of the securities are issued in France and 41% abroad, with the remaining 18% being fund units that cannot be allocated.

The banks-and-insurers link is worth noting. A large part of insurers' holdings are claims on the financial sector, so the health of banks and insurers is interconnected, which is a recurrent theme in financial-stability analysis. The source does not discuss that risk, but the data show its scale.

A methodology note affects how the series should be read. From the first quarter of 2025, the series includes an estimate of foreign fund holdings, which reduces the unallocated share of fund units. The scope also now covers directly held deposits and loans and indirect real estate holdings through funds. Comparisons with older data should take this into account.

How should readers interpret valuation losses? A valuation loss is a change in the market value of assets that insurers still hold, not cash lost. For a life insurer holding bonds to maturity to meet long-term obligations, a fall in market price does not necessarily mean a realised loss, because the bond will still pay its coupons and its face value at maturity unless the issuer defaults. Rising rates also allow insurers to reinvest maturing bonds and new premiums at higher yields, which supports future returns and the ability to pay guaranteed or declared returns on policies. The downside is that higher rates can encourage policyholders to move savings elsewhere, and if insurers had to sell bonds at a loss to meet withdrawals, the paper losses would become real. The Banque de France data do not indicate that this occurred, and they only record asset values and flows.

For French savers, the main route to this market is life insurance, a very popular savings product in France. The returns credited to policyholders depend partly on what insurers earn on their portfolios, so persistent increases in interest rates feed through gradually as insurers reinvest. The data do not address policyholder returns or surrenders, so no conclusion can be drawn on those from this release alone.

For the wider economy, French insurers are significant buyers of government and corporate debt, and also fund companies through equity. Net purchases of €20.9 billion of long-term debt in a single quarter show how much they contribute to financing. Weaker prices for existing holdings do not stop them from buying; in fact, higher yields may make debt more attractive.

The October 6 publication will show whether valuation effects reversed or deepened in the second quarter, depending on how rates and share prices moved. Readers following the French insurance sector can use these quarterly statistics as a simple way to see how rate moves translate into portfolio values.

why_it_matters: French insurers are among Europe's largest institutional investors, and the savings of millions of households sit in their portfolios. When rates rise, bond values drop on paper even as new money earns higher yields, so these figures show how interest-rate moves feed through to life insurance returns and to the funds insurers lend to governments and companies.
